sweep_summary: Two title hits for Awa (PNG), both resolved. (1) Scheer 2008 (prosodic hierarchy as a diacritic) is a general syntax-phonology-interface paper attached to Awa only by Glottolog's own 'computerized assignment from \"must\"'; not about Awa, not read (HAL metadata-only, Elsevier chapter gated), priority none. (2) McPherson 2016, Language 92(1) e38-e66: obtained the author's open final manuscript from her Dartmouth page (saved as + extracted text). The Glottolog title 'Culminativity' is a typo for 'Cumulativity' (HG constraint ganging), so the accent-keyword hit is spurious; the paper contains no stress or accent-placement claim at all. It reanalyses Loving 1973's tone data and states that Awa 'is a tonal language with a fairly high functional load in both lexical and grammatical distinctions', four tones H/HL/LH/L reduced to H and L primitives — confirming the catalog's 'tonal' coding (deciding source Loving 1966/1973, which stays in force; McPherson is secondary and does not supersede it). Side note from the on-disk McKaughan & Loving 1973 morphology text (rosettaproject_awb_morsyn-2, §2.1.5): 'Additional emphasis may be given by laying extra stress on the suffix.. -de receiving strong stress' — pragmatic emphasis on an emphatic clitic, not lexical word stress; no change to the classification. all lookups went through direct downloads (Cambridge, Crossref, HAL, Glottolog, Semantic Scholar API, author page). and updated at

new_statements.quote: Awa (ISO 639-3: awb) is a Papuan language in the Kainantu group spoken in the Eastern Highlands region of Papua New Guinea by about 2000 people. It is a tonal language with a fairly high functional load in both lexical and grammatical distinctions. [...] Awa is described as having four tones, high (H), falling (HL), rising (LH) and low (L). Though Loving lists these as equal tonemes, I will show in this analysis that HL and LH are best seen as the combination of L and H rather than as tonal primitives in their own right. The tonal primitives are linked to syllables, and each syllable can carry up to two tones.

new_statements.reading: Awa is a lexical- and grammatical-tone language; four surface tones (H, HL, LH, L), analysed as H/L primitives with up to two tones per syllable and rises confined to phrase-final syllables. The paper says nothing about stress, so it confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding without adding a stress statement. It is a secondary reanalysis of Loving's 1966/1973 data, not first-hand fieldwork; Loving 1966 (= Loving 1973 reprint already held by the project) remains the primary deciding source.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Awa is described purely as a toneme language: every syllable carries exactly one of four tonemes (high, falling, rising, low), contrastive on any syllable of the word (rising excluded from non-final syllables). The chapter has no stress, accent or prominence section and never uses the word 'stress'; the only 'stress' in Part One is a remark in Loving & Loving's noun-suffix chapter that extra emphasis can be given 'by laying extra stress on the suffix' -de (rosettaproject_awb_morsyn-2, §2.1.5), which is pragmatic emphasis, not a word-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: none (tone only); rising toneme does not occur word-initially or medially
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Awa of the Lamari River area (Eastern Highlands), Loving's fieldwork variety; McKaughan 1973 Part One also contains a chapter 'The dialects of Awa' (not scanned by the Rosetta Project, not read). Note that the Rosetta Project 'awb' item list mixes in Colombian Awa-Cuaiquer items (Fonologia del cuaiquer, Una gramatica pedagogica del cuaiquer), which are a different language (Barbacoan) and were not used.

new_statements.quote: 3. Syllable-based tone. The Eastern New Guinea Highlands group tends to have tonal languages, such as Gadsup, Binumarien, Siane, Awa, Kanite, etc. which may contrast tone on any syllable (see McKaughan [1973] for several of these). 3.1 Awa. Awa (Trans-New Guinea; Loving 1973) exhibits High, Low, Rising, and Falling tones, and these may contrast on any syllable. In monosyllabic forms, one finds all these tones. In di- and trisyllabic words, Rising tones occur only word-finally. In disyllabic words, ten out of the sixteen possible combinations are found. In trisyllabic words, all contrasts are found word-finally, and all but Rising contrast word-initially.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Cahill classifies Awa as a syllable-based tone language (tone contrastive on every syllable, four tones H/L/R/F, rising only phrase-finally, no adjacent falling tones, tone sandhi with rising->low plus H shift to the next word). He says nothing about stress or accent in Awa; his stress/pitch accent discussion concerns other PNG languages (Yimas, Korafe, Tinputz, Kairi, Fore, Kamano-Yagaria).

tone_statements.quote: Awa tonemes include high, falling, rising, and low. In this dictionary low, which occurs most frequently, is unwritten, high is indicated by ´, falling by ˆ, and rising by ˇ placed over the appropriate vowel. Rising tonemes are heard phonetically as low mid tonemes word medially. In phrases tonemes are written on words in the form in which they occur as a result of tonal perturbation and not as they would occur on words in isolation. ... For more detail on the phonemes of Awa see Loving 1966.
tone_statements.summary: Four tonemes (high, falling, rising, low) marked in the orthography; rising heard as low-mid word-medially; phrase forms show tone sandhi; p. vii: affix tone varies by stem. Refers to Loving 1966.

sources.quote: 'The phonological description concerns segmental and prosodic features, but does not deal with units larger than the syllable. ... Tone in New Guinea languages has now been attested in many cases. Awa has a four-tone system - high, falling, rising, and low. Though these tones are easily contrasted in lexical environments, the functional load is not seemingly as high as for the more commonly known tone languages. ... High tones step gradually up in a sequence, and low tones step gradually down. ... Tone perturbation obscures the basic lexical tone when items occur in phrases or sentences.' No s

sources.quote: In their phonologies, the East-Central Family languages show a strong development of supra-segmental features manifesting themselves in tonal systems and combined tone-stress systems. The glottal stop phoneme appears with extremely high statistical frequency in the languages of the Gahuku and the Kamano Sub-Families, and in Gimi.

sources.note: States that the East-Central Family languages (Gende, Siane, Yabiyufa, Gahuku, Asaro, Benabena, Kamano group, Yagaria, Fore, Gimi) show a strong development of suprasegmental features -- tonal systems and combined tone-stress systems; illustrative tone detail is given only for Awa (Eastern Family: four tonemes) and Yagaria, none for Yabiyufa itself. Consistent with (does not contradict) the two-register-tone statement listed here.

sources.quote: Awa tonemes include high, falling, rising, and low. In this dictionary low, which occurs most frequently, is unwritten, high is indicated by ´, falling by ˆ, and rising by ˇ placed over the appropriate vowel. Rising tonemes are heard phonetically as low mid tonemes word medially. In phrases tonemes are written on words in the form in which they occur as a result of tonal perturbation and not as they would occur on words in isolation. ... For more detail on the phonemes of Awa see Loving 1966.
sources.note: Four tonemes (high, falling, rising, low) marked in the orthography; rising heard as low-mid word-medially; phrase forms show tone sandhi; p. vii: affix tone varies by stem. Refers to Loving 1966.
